title: Strength
summary:
Strength training in pregnancy, once worried over for safety, is presented as useful when supervised, done with moderate loads and good technique. It supports the extra muscular demands of pregnancy (added body weight, a shifted center of gravity, looser ligaments and the need for postural stability), helps with back pain and posture, and prepares the body for labor and postpartum recovery.

The chapter describes exercise types: moderate-load work with modifications, strength endurance, bodyweight and isometric stabilization, and aquatic training. It stresses progressive overload aimed at maintenance and function rather than maximal strength, combined with aerobic work and adjusted by trimester. Three sample second-trimester programs are given for sedentary, active and advanced women, and all training should follow a medical evaluation.
points: In a supervised 12-week low-to-moderate program of 32 pregnant women, strength rose 36% (leg press), 39% (leg curl), 41% (lumbar extension) and 56% (leg extension), and lumbar endurance about 14%.
In that study no musculoskeletal injuries occurred, adverse symptoms were under 2% of sessions, and blood pressure stayed unchanged.

Strength training may help manage excessive gestational weight gain, improve insulin sensitivity and glucose profile, and reduce gestational diabetes risk, though direct evidence for strength alone is less extensive.
Strength endurance work uses 12-20 repetitions, two to three sets, with bands or 1-5 kg weights, emphasizing core, glutes, lower back and legs.
Isometric work uses 20-30 repetitions or 30-40 s holds, for example modified planks, bird dog and glute bridge with pause.
Modifications include goblet squats instead of back squats, incline or seated presses instead of flat bench in later trimesters, and avoiding Olympic lifts without experience and supervision.
Avoid prolonged supine positions after the first trimester and limit Valsalva maneuvers.
The second trimester is usually most favorable; in the third, reduce maximum loads, increase stability and watch balance.
Sample programs: sedentary 2-3 sessions/week, 20-30 min, RPE 11-13; active 3-4 sessions, 30-40 min, RPE 12-14; advanced 4-5 sessions, 40-60 min, RPE 13-15.
takeaways: Get a medical evaluation and individual adjustments before starting.
Start with light-to-moderate loads, prioritize technique and progress by tolerance.
Aim for maintenance and functionality, not maximal strength or hypertrophy.
Build the week around basic patterns: vertical and horizontal pulls and pushes, hip-dominant and knee-dominant movements.
Combine strength with aerobic exercise, and include recovery, mobility and core days.
Beginners can progress to three sets, 15-20 repetitions, and add light weight after 4-6 weeks.
cautions: Avoid excessive Valsalva maneuvers and excessive strain, and keep hydrated and monitor heart rate.
Avoid prolonged supine positions after the first trimester and exercises that compress the abdomen or reduce venous return.
Watch for warning signs and fatigue; avoid high-impact exercise and Olympic lifts without experience and supervision.
